elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause contains no affiliate carve-out; the only no-consent exception is "to a successor organization by merger, consolidation or acquisition." An affiliate transfer would still require the other party's prior written consent.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: The carve-out covers a "successor organization by merger, consolidation or acquisition" only; a sale of substantially all assets is not among the listed triggers, so an asset-sale successor would fall back into the consent requirement.

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: "Neither party will assign this Agreement or any of its rights hereunder without the prior written consent of the other party" now binds IBM as well as Customer.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: "...such consent not to be unreasonably withheld" applies symmetrically to consent given by either party, including Customer's consent to an IBM assignment.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: No competitor bar appears in the rendered text; IBM may assign to a Customer competitor if Customer's consent is obtained (and consent may not be unreasonably withheld), with no absolute prohibition.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply on the record before me: the cited assignment provision contains no change-of-control, deemed-assignment, or re-pricing trigger, and the finding records that no change-of-control clause exists elsewhere, so no Vendor termination right arises on Customer's change of control.

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: "[E]ither party may assign this Agreement, upon written notice to the other party, to a successor organization by merger, consolidation or acquisition."

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: The successor carve-out is expressly conditioned "upon written notice to the other party."

"Neither party will assign this Agreement or any of its rights hereunder without the prior written consent of the other party"; no residual no-consent exception (no affiliate or other non-successor carve-out) is retained, and attempted assignments in violation are void.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: "...such consent not to be unreasonably withheld" attaches directly to the general consent requirement applicable to both parties.

reasons: Fallback checklist is complete on the operative language: mutual successor right on written notice, consent required for all other assignments, and a not-unreasonably-withheld standard binding both parties.

Preferred level is not reached: there is no affiliate carve-out, the successor trigger omits a sale of substantially all assets, and there is no absolute bar on IBM assigning to a Customer competitor. To reach preferred, the drafter would need to add "to an affiliate or" and "or sale of substantially all of its assets" to the Customer carve-out and add an express prohibition on IBM assigning to a competitor of Customer.

Minimality holds: the only edits are the two operative sentences needed to make the clause mutual and to add the notice mechanic; the void-assignment sentence and the continuing-liability sentence are retained verbatim, and no survival tails, expense language, or extra procedures were added.

Intent preserved: no undefined terms or dangling cross-references are created. The retained final sentence ("Customer will remain liable for its obligations hereunder") remains accurate and is not contradicted by the new mutual language; it is Customer-adverse but was left unchanged, which is the correct minimal treatment.
Residual risk after the redline is limited to preferred-level gaps (affiliate transfers and a competitor assignee), so the deviation classification is correct but its severity is moderated.
